questions.q: Name the symbols used for a cell, bulb, switch and battery in circuits.
questions.a: Cell: long-short parallel lines; bulb: circle with cross; switch: break with lever; battery: cell symbols in series.

questions.q: Why do we draw circuit diagrams with symbols?
questions.a: Symbols make diagrams neat, quick to draw and understood by everyone.

questions.q: What does an open switch do to a circuit?
questions.a: It breaks the path, so no current flows and the bulb stays off.

questions.q: What is an electric battery?
questions.a: Two or more cells joined in series to give higher voltage.

questions.q: Why do we combine cells in a torch?
questions.a: Two or more cells together give more current and a brighter light than one cell.

questions.q: What decides which cell terminal connects where?
questions.a: Current flows from the positive terminal through the circuit back to the negative terminal.

questions.q: What is a closed circuit?
questions.a: A complete, unbroken path from one cell terminal to the other, letting current flow and the bulb glow.

questions.q: What is an open circuit?
questions.a: A broken path (switch off, loose wire) where no current flows.

questions.q: Why does a bulb not glow when a wire is loose?
questions.a: The gap stops the current path, so no electricity flows through the filament.

questions.q: Why does a bulb's filament glow?
questions.a: Current heats the thin filament till it glows white-hot, giving light.

questions.q: What happens to the heating when the current is increased?
questions.a: More current means more heat - the filament glows brighter (and can burn out).

questions.q: Name a device that uses the heating effect of current.
questions.a: Electric heater, iron, toaster or fuse.

questions.q: On what factors does heat produced in a wire depend?
questions.a: The current, the wire's resistance (material, length, thickness) and the time current flows.

questions.q: Why does a thin wire heat more than a thick one for the same current?
questions.a: A thin wire has higher resistance, so more heat is produced.

questions.q: Which metal wires conduct with least heating?
questions.a: Thick copper wires - low resistance means little heat loss.

questions.q: What is an electric fuse?
questions.a: A short wire of low-melting metal in the circuit that melts when current is too high, breaking it.

questions.q: How does a fuse protect appliances?
questions.a: It melts before excess current can overheat wiring or burn the appliance.

questions.q: What decides the rating of a fuse?
questions.a: The safe current limit of the circuit - the fuse wire must melt just above it.

questions.q: What is the magnetic effect of electric current?
questions.a: A current-carrying wire acts like a magnet, deflecting a nearby compass needle.

questions.q: How can you show a wire carries current using a compass?
questions.a: Place the compass near the wire - deflection of the needle shows current is flowing.

questions.q: Who discovered the magnetic effect of current?
questions.a: Hans Christian Oersted in 1820.

questions.q: What is an electromagnet?
questions.a: A coil wound on soft iron that acts as a magnet only while current flows through the coil.

questions.q: How can an electromagnet be made stronger?
questions.a: More turns of wire, more current, or a better iron core.

questions.q: State one advantage of an electromagnet over a permanent magnet.
questions.a: It can be switched on and off, and its strength is adjustable.

questions.q: How does an electric bell work?
questions.a: Current makes the electromagnet attract an iron strip; the hammer strikes the gong and the circuit breaks, repeating rapidly.

questions.q: Why does the bell ring continuously while the switch is on?
questions.a: The circuit breaks and remakes each time the hammer moves, so the gong is struck again and again.

questions.q: What is the role of the contact screw in an electric bell?
questions.a: It completes the circuit when the strip springs back, restarting the cycle.
